title: Exploring How Multiple Levels of GPT-Generated Programming Hints Support or Disappoint Novices
venue: CHI EA '24: Extended Abstracts of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different levels of GPT-generated programming hints affect novice learners’ problem-solving and learning in introductory programming. The authors note that most LLM-based hint systems provide only one kind of hint, typically high-level natural language guidance, and ask whether multiple levels of hints—from general guidance to concrete code support—better match students’ needs during programming tasks.

To study this, the authors designed the "LLM Hint Factory," a system that generates four levels of hints for each help request: orientation hints, instrumental hints, worked-example hints, and bottom-out hints. They conducted an IRB-approved think-aloud study with 12 novice programming learners who completed three Python data-analysis tasks, along with identical pre- and post-tests and a structured interview. The system was used in a controlled one-hour session, and the authors also performed an expert evaluation of hint quality across dimensions such as appropriateness, targeting, comprehensibility, and alignment.

The participants were undergraduate and graduate students in the United States who were currently enrolled in, or had only taken, introductory computer science courses for non-majors using Python. The context was a study session using programming tasks adapted from coursework at two U.S. universities. The work focused on novice students seeking on-demand AI-generated help while solving CS1-style problems.

The main conclusion is that high-level natural language hints alone were often insufficient and could sometimes be misleading or frustrating, especially for next-step logic, next-step syntax, and debugging syntax requests. Lower-level hints—particularly worked-example code with inline comments—were more effective in helping students make correct code changes and learn relevant concepts. The authors argue that future AI tutoring systems should personalize help responses by varying content, format, and granularity to better match students’ immediate help-seeking context.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here to generate multi-level programming hints in the LLM Hint Factory.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the LLM Hint Factory to generate four levels of on-demand programming hints for novice Python learners: orientation, instrumental, worked example, and bottom-out hints during CS1 problem solving.

findings.finding_summary: In a think-aloud study with 12 novice programming learners, expert review of sampled hints found overall high formal quality for GPT-generated hints: 81.91% appropriate, 99.67% targeted, and 98.36% comprehensible. However, among expert-labeled high-quality hints, 77.78% helped students move forward correctly, 1.43% were misunderstood and led to negative effects, and 27.14% had no observable impact on progression.
findings.measure: Expert evaluation of hint quality; observed correctness/progression after hint use during programming tasks

findings.finding_summary: Lower-level GPT-generated hints were more effective than high-level natural-language hints for supporting novice programming actions. Among expert-labeled appropriate hints, students made correct code changes in 35 instances (59.32%) after reaching the worked-example hint level and in 5 instances after receiving bottom-out hints; for students who improved from pre- to post-test, 75% were satisfied with worked-example hints and 25% needed bottom-out hints.
findings.measure: Correct code changes during learning session; pre- to post-test programming improvements

findings.finding_summary: High-level GPT-generated natural-language hints alone were often insufficient and could be misleading, especially for next-step or syntax-related help requests, while worked-example code hints better supported these cases. By contrast, high-level hints were often sufficient for debugging logic errors, and 33.3% of students (n=4) reported frustration when high-level hints repeated information they already knew.
findings.measure: Help-request resolution by hint level/type; student interview reports of helpfulness and frustration

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical think-aloud user study with pre/post testing and expert hint evaluation, but it uses a very small sample (n=12) and lacks a controlled experimental comparison or reported inferential effect estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising but largely descriptive evidence that worked-example and bottom-out GPT hints can improve novice programming support relative to high-level hints, but effects are not quantified with standard effect sizes and results are mixed in some conditions.
